chunks: Abu Ali al-Ash'ari, from Muhammad ibn Abd al-Jabbar, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shazan, all from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked him (peace be upon him) about the ornamented swords in which there is silver, can they be sold for gold to a specified term? He (peace be upon him) said: 'The people did not differ regarding the credit (sale on deferred payment) that it is usury (riba). They only differed regarding 'hand to hand' (cash) transactions.' I said to him (peace be upon him): 'So can it be sold for dirhams in cash?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'My father (peace be upon him) used to say: It is more beloved to me if there is something else (a commodity) along with it.' I said to him (peace be upon him): 'When the dirhams given are more than the silver contained in the sword?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And how is the precaution for them with that?' I said to him (peace be upon him): 'Because they claim that they recognize that (the value difference).' He (peace be upon him) said: 'If they recognize that, then there is no problem; otherwise, it is more beloved to me if they include something else (a commodity) along with it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on selling silver-inlaid swords for gold on credit or for cash?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the Shia juristic distinction between 'hand-to-hand' (cash) and 'credit' exchanges in gold-silver transactions, highlighting the Imam's preference for including an additional commodity ('ard) to mitigate uncertainty in valuation. It reflects the scholarly debate on whether equal weight suffices for cash sales or if actual value parity is required, emphasizing caution against hidden usury. The Imam’s advice underscores the practical application of avoiding riba by ensuring transparency in commodity-based exchanges rather than relying on assumed knowledge of intrinsic worth.
